---
title: "Handbook on utilising new data sources in the production of consumer price statistics"
---

This Handbook provides an overview and reference framework for the use of new data sources in the production of consumer price statistics.\

Developed by the [UN Task Team on Scanner Data](https://unstats.un.org/bigdata/task-teams/scanner/index.cshtml), it is intended for a broad audience, including national statistical offices, central banks, international organisations, and researchers involved in the development, implementation, or evaluation of consumer price indices. 

The Handbook covers a broad range of data sources - including transaction data such as scanner data, and non-transaction data such as web-scraped data - that differ to traditional collection in how prices are observed, recorded and accessed. It is intended to support both organisations exploring these data sources for the first time, and those seeking to refine or extend existing implementations.

This Handbook complements Chapter 10 of the [CPI Manual, Concepts and Methods](https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/%40dgreports/%40stat/documents/publication/wcms_761444.pdf) by providing detailed operational guidance on the use of alternative data sources in CPI production. It does not replace the CPI Manual, which sets out the underlying concepts, principles and governance framework for the use of alternative data sources in CPI compilation. 

This Handbook covers key stages of the CPI production process where new data sources may be introduced, including data acquisition, preparation, classification, index compilation, quality assurance, and dissemination. It brings together conceptual discussion, practical considerations, methodological options, and examples from country practices, with the aim of supporting informed decision-making rather than prescribing a single method or workflow.

There is no single "correct" approach to using new data sources in CPI production. The appropriate choices will depend on national circumstances, data availability, institutional arrangements, technical capacity, and user needs. Accordingly, the purpose of this handbook is to present the range of available approaches, highlight their strengths and limitations, and provide guidance to help users assess what is most suitable for their particular context.

While the primary focus of this Handbook is on consumer price statistics, many of the data sources, processes, and systems discussed may also support other areas of official statistics. Where relevant, considerations for broader statistical use are highlighted to support efficient and sustainable use of alternative data sources across statistical domains.

This Handbook draws on existing international manuals, methodological papers, and country experiences, while also improving the literature on topics where guidance is currently more limited, such as data acquisition strategies, classification challenges, and the handling of highly dynamic product universes. Given the rapid pace of methodological and technological developments in this field, the handbook is designed as a living document. It will be reviewed and updated over time to reflect new research, emerging best practices, and feedback from users.

Users of this Handbook are encouraged to support its ongoing development and improvement. Feedback may include suggestions on topics that could be expanded or added, identification of errors or areas requiring clarification, or proposals to refine existing content in light of new research or country experience. Such feedback will help ensure that this Handbook remains relevant, accurate, and responsive to the evolving needs of the international statistical community. Feedback can be provided through answering the questions on this form: [UN Task Team on Scanner Data - e-Handbook Feedback Form](https://forms.office.com/Pages/ResponsePage.aspx?id=vweIB4LOiEa84A2BFoTcRidRNcIM9HtMhJmbNi1T8MlUNTZXQ0MzUk5RQTNQMlUzWldETDJaR0JSQy4u&r3ba99449c6ab4175bd4fd934b09149a5=https%3A%2F%2Funstats.un.org%2Fwiki%2Fspaces%2FGWGSD%2Fpages%2F240910447%2FHandbook%2Bon%2Butilising%2Bnew%2Bdata%2Bsources%2Bin%2Bthe%2Bproduction%2Bof%2Bconsumer%2Bprice%2Bstatistics).

This Handbook is publicly available and intended to be used alongside related [training materials](training-material.qmd) and other supporting resources developed by the UN Task Team on Scanner Data.

# Contents: {#Handbookonutilisingnewdatasourcesintheproductionofconsumerpricestatistics-Contents}

- [Acknowledgements](acknowledgements.qmd) --- The development of this handbook and associated training material is a testament to the hard work of many individuals who collaborated on drafting, reviewing and updating the content. 
- [Glossary](glossary.qmd) --- This page contains the handbook glossary.
- [Initial considerations](initial-considerations.qmd) --- This section covers some initial considerations that NSOs are recommended to review before setting out to use alternative data sources in the production of consumer price statistics.
  - [Overview of alternative data sources](overview-of-alternative-data-sources.qmd) --- This page contains a general introduction to each of the alternative data sources used to compile consumer price indices. 
  - [Why use alternative data sources? Strategic motivations](why-use-alternative-data-sources-strategic-motivations.qmd) --- Common reasons shared by NSOs as a driver for using these new data sources.
  - [Key challenges and trade-offs](key-challenges-and-trade-offs.qmd) --- Alternative data sources introduce a number of challenges and trade-offs that National Statistical Offices (NSOs) must actively manage.
  - [Key decision points](key-decision-points.qmd) --- The adoption of alternative data sources involves a sequence of related decisions that shape both the technical and organisational direction of implementation.
  - [Resource implications and organisational readiness](resource-implications-and-organisational-readiness.qmd) --- The adoption of alternative data sources typically requires a different mix of resources and capabilities compared with traditional survey-based price collection.
- [CPI production system requirements](cpi-production-system-requirements.qmd) --- Requirements for IT systems are dependent on the choice of data source, the implementation plan for each new data source and the availability and knowledge of staff with specialist IT skills. 
- [Quality assurance](quality-assurance.qmd) --- The use of alternative data sources in CPI compilation requires robust quality assurance procedures. 
- [Data selection and acquisition](data-selection-and-acquisition.qmd) --- This section discusses how to select and acquire these new data sources.
  - [Selection of categories](selection-of-categories.qmd) --- One of the initial steps in this process is the identification and selection of product categories to consider for the adoption of alternative data sources
  - [Selection of retailers for alternative data sources](selection-of-retailers-for-alternative-data-sources.qmd) --- This page contains information on how to identify suitable retailers who can supply these alternative data sources
  - [Scanner data](scanner-data.qmd) --- This section addresses the main steps that should be considered for acquisition of scanner data sets for the production of price statistics.
    - [Initial steps in the acquisition of scanner data](initial-steps-in-the-acquisition-of-scanner-data.qmd) --- Recommendations on how an NSO can approach retailers to acquire scanner data
    - [Data requirements specification for scanner data](data-requirements-specification-for-scanner-data.qmd) --- Key variables to ask for when acquiring scanner data.
    - [Data sharing agreements](data-sharing-agreements.qmd) --- Data sharing agreements can help provide structure to data flows between a supplier and NSO
    - [Alternative approaches to acquiring scanner data](alternative-approaches-to-acquiring-scanner-data.qmd) --- Suggestions of what to do if the NSO is unable to acquire scanner data directly from retailers
    - [Monitoring, validation and plausibility checks for scanner data](monitoring-validation-and-plausibility-checks-for-scanner-data.qmd) --- Recommended checks to carry out on the incoming flows of scanner data
  - [Web scraping](web-scraping.qmd) --- This section covers the acquisition of web scraped data.
    - [Different approaches to accessing web scraped data](different-approaches-to-accessing-web-scraped-data.qmd) --- Approaches for setting up a web scraping project
    - [Strategies available for in-house web scraping](strategies-available-for-in-house-web-scraping.qmd) --- Points to consider if in-house web scraping is the chosen solution
    - [Data requirements specification for web scraped data](data-requirements-specification-for-web-scraped-data.qmd) --- Key variables to look for when acquiring web scraped data
    - [Monitoring, validation and plausibility checks for web scraped data](monitoring-validation-and-plausibility-checks-for-web-scraped-data.qmd) --- Recommended checks to carry out on incoming flows of web scraping data
    - [Common technical problems for in-house web scraping](common-technical-problems-for-in-house-web-scraping.qmd) --- Overcoming some common technical problems for web scraping
  - [Example file structures for web scraped and scanner data](example-file-structures-for-web-scraped-and-scanner-data.qmd) --- This page contains example variables and data types for new data sources
  - [Collection of data via APIs](collection-of-data-via-apis.qmd) --- An alternative to automatically scraping data from web pages is to extract data directly from application programming interface (APIs)
  - [Dealing with unexpected data gaps](dealing-with-unexpected-data-gaps.qmd) --- This page contains information on how to deal with unexpected gaps in the supply of new data sources
- [Preparation of data](preparation-of-data.qmd) --- This sections summarises the general steps required to prepare these new data sources for use in price index compilation.
  - [Product sampling for price index calculation](product-sampling-for-price-index-calculation.qmd) --- NSOs can either choose to use all available data from their new data source, or to use a sample of this data. 
  - [Standardising the data](standardising-the-data.qmd) --- Data will need to be standardised before being used to calculate price indices.
  - [Aggregation across time and outlets](aggregation-across-time-and-outlets.qmd) --- Data are usually disaggregated by various dimensions. This page contains information on how products can be aggregated across time and outlets.
  - [Identifying unique products](identifying-unique-products.qmd) --- Data are usually disaggregated by various dimensions. This page contains information on how products can be defined from the given article codes.
  - [Treatment of discounts and refunds](treatment-of-discounts-and-refunds.qmd) --- This page contains information on how discounts and refunds should be treated in the data.
- [Classification](classification.qmd) --- The goal of this section is to provide guidance on the critical step of classifying new data sources and make them ready for price index compilation. 
  - [Pre-conditions and deciding on appropriate classification methods](pre-conditions-and-deciding-on-appropriate-classification-methods.qmd) --- There are several factors that NSO typically consider when approaching or implementing classification, such as the scale and complexity of the task, whether this is just the initial phase of classification or recurrent classification in production, or the structure and quality of the data. Evaluating these factors is useful to select the method(s) most appropriate for each use case.
    - [Note on variables applicable for classification](note-on-variables-applicable-for-classification.qmd) --- Several variables obtained during the acquisition process  are typically applicable for classification. 
  - [Method 0: Manual labelling or validation of predicted labels](method-0-manual-labelling-or-validation-of-predicted-labels.qmd) --- Manual classification involves each unique product being manually assigned a classification class. This is often described as labelling, and those who specialize in the task, labellers This method can also be used to validate classification done automatically by other methods. 
  - [Method 1: Attribute-based classification method](method-1-attribute-based-classification-method.qmd) --- Attribute-based classification involves classifying observations in the data by mapping structured variables or attributes available in the alternative data file to the necessary taxonomy classes. 
  - [Method 2: Pattern matching classification method](method-2-pattern-matching-classification-method.qmd) --- Pattern based classification involves mapping individual records to the taxonomy classes of interest according to patterns present in their descriptive attributes. For instance, patterns in the categories of the alternative data, patterns in the product name, or specific keywords in the product description - could all be used to classify a set of individual records. 
  - [Method 3: Recommendation / Machine-assisted classification](method-3-recommendation-machine-assisted-classification.qmd) --- Machine-assisted classification is still a manual classification technique and therefore the ideas in the manual classification chapter are still valid. The key difference is the addition of a recommendation system that supports labellers in identifying the most appropriate class. Every product is still manually scrutinised, but machine-assistance may improve efficiency and potentially quality by offering recommendations. 
  - [Method 4: Machine Learning classification method](method-4-machine-learning-classification-method.qmd) --- Machine Learning (ML) can be a stable solution for classifying unique products when an NSO starts to use new data sources at scale. NSOs typically use supervised ML methods whereby a manually annotated dataset is used to train a classifier to predict all new unique products as part of recurrent classification. 
    - [How to evaluate classification methods](how-to-evaluate-classification-methods.qmd) --- There are numerous metrics that can be tracked and applied when evaluating how well a classifier performs. 
    - [Working with class imbalance](working-with-class-imbalance.qmd) --- Datasets NSOs need to classify are typically not equally distributed, as some classes have many records (i.e. unique products) while others have only a few. This requires additional steps to be taken when designing and testing classifiers. 
  - [Operational best practices](operational-best-practices.qmd) --- Once NSOs select and develop an appropriate classification method, they have to implement it. This section includes articles on appropriate ways to operationalize classification. 
    - [Designing the classification step: operational considerations](designing-the-classification-step-operational-considerations.qmd) --- This section provides context about where and how the classification step fits into the rest of the pipeline processing alternative data to create elementary price indices, as well as some important considerations and options when setting up the classification process. This article can also be seen as a companion to the pre-conditions to classification section, helping the NSO design the operational process for the individual or blended method that will be chosen.
- [Data filtering and missing prices](data-filtering-and-missing-prices.qmd) --- This section covers some common methods used to filter the data before it is used to calculate indices, as well as a summary of how missing prices should be treated.
  - [Outlier filter](outlier-filter.qmd) --- Outlier filters aim at excluding or correcting extreme price increases or price decreases, typically compared to the previous period, from the price index calculation
  - [Dumping filter](dumping-filter.qmd) --- Dumping filters aim at eliminating the downward pressure of clearance prices on the index.
  - [Low sales filter](low-sales-filter.qmd) --- The low sales filter ensures that products with small expenditure shares do not unduly influence the index results.
  - [Current practice of data filtering](current-practice-of-data-filtering.qmd) --- This page contains a summary of how NSOs currently approach data filtering.
  - [Treatment of missing prices](treatment-of-missing-prices.qmd) --- This page contains information on how to treat missing prices through product-level imputation methods.
- [Price index methods](price-index-methods.qmd) --- This section summarises the current literature available on price index methods that can be used for these new data sources.
  - [Bilateral price index methods](bilateral-price-index-methods.qmd) --- This section presents the basic, commonly known formulas of bilateral price indices. 
    - [Example of chain drift](example-of-chain-drift.qmd) --- Chain drift occurs when an index does not return to unity when prices in the current period return to their levels in the base period. 
  - [Multilateral price index methods](multilateral-price-index-methods.qmd) --- This section presents the basic, commonly known formulas of multilateral price indices.
  - [Extension methods](extension-methods.qmd) --- Extension methods can be used in combination with multilateral methods to ensure revision-free index series. 
  - [Decomposition](decomposition.qmd) --- In addition to measuring the aggregate price or quantity change, it is important to decompose the change into its contributions by individual commodities or groupings.
  - [Choosing an index method](choosing-an-index-method.qmd) --- This section contains information on how an NSO can choose a suitable index method.
    - [Methods for when expenditure data are available](methods-for-when-expenditure-data-are-available.qmd) --- This page summarizes potential criteria that could be used by an NSO to decide on an index method for when expenditure data are available.
    - [Methods for when expenditure data are not available](methods-for-when-expenditure-data-are-not-available.qmd) --- This page summarises potential criteria that could be used by an NSO to decide on an index method for when expenditure data are not available.
  - [Deriving proxy weights for web scraped data](deriving-proxy-weights-for-web-scraped-data.qmd) --- Web scraped data does not contain expenditure information. In some cases, proxy expenditure weights can be derived.
- [Aggregation](aggregation.qmd) --- This page contains information on how alternative data sources can be aggregated with existing data sources
- [Other uses of alternative data](other-uses-of-alternative-data.qmd) --- This section briefly outlines additional uses of alternative data sources, both within CPI production and across other areas of official statistics, to help NSOs consider the broader value of data acquisition and integration efforts.
  - [Other uses of alternative data beyond CPI](other-uses-of-alternative-data-beyond-cpi.qmd) --- Beyond CPI production, many of the data sources and processes described in this handbook may also support a range of other official statistical domains.
  - [Other uses of alternative data within CPI](other-uses-of-alternative-data-within-cpi.qmd) --- While much of this handbook focuses on the use of alternative data sources for the calculation of price indices, these data may also support other aspects of CPI production.
- [Other considerations](other-considerations.qmd) --- This section contains information on how to treat seasonal products and quality change.
  - [Seasonal products](seasonal-products.qmd) --- This page contains information on the treatment of seasonal products in the CPI and implications of using the new data sources
  - [Quality change and hedonic estimation](quality-change-and-hedonic-estimation.qmd) --- This page contains information on accounting for quality change in the measurement of consumer prices
- [Implementation](implementation.qmd) --- This page contains information on how to implement these new data sources into production. 
- [Training material](training-material.qmd) --- This page contains a summary of the planned training curriculum and links to available courses.
